<div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/jackson3-1024x769.png" title="Image by Thomas Jackson." alt="Image by Thomas Jackson." /></div></div>



<p>Fabrics flutter in seemingly impossible ways in artist <a href="https://thomasjacksonphotography.com/">Thomas Jackson</a>&#8216;s images. But despite first appearances, each photograph is true to life; the fabrics are suspended on taut lines. Their <a href="/2012/08/the-flapping-of-flexible-objects-like-flags-have/">dance</a> is driven by wind energy, drag, tension, and flow&#8211;not manipulated pixels. I love the (turbulent) energy of them! (Image credit: <a href="https://thomasjacksonphotography.com/">T. Jackson</a>; via <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/03/thomas-jackson-fabrics-landscapes-photographs/?__readwiseLocation=">Colossal</a>)</p>

		<item>
		<title>Recreating Atmospheres</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/recreating-atmospheres/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/recreating-atmospheres/#comments</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 30 Apr 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[atmospheric science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[energy cascade]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[flow visualization]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[planetary science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[rotating flow]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[turbulence]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[vorticity]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=29751</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[In planetary atmospheres, energy and vorticity can cascade from large scales to smaller ones, but the mechanics of this transfer remain somewhat elusive. In a recent experiment, researchers built a lab-scale representation of an atmosphere using a meter-scale rotating annular tank. The outer bottom edge of the tank gets heated&#8211;representing the sun&#8217;s warming at the [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p>In planetary atmospheres, energy and <a href="/tagged/vorticity/">vorticity</a> can cascade from large scales to smaller ones, but the mechanics of this transfer remain somewhat elusive. In a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/n2nj-dg5r">recent experiment</a>, researchers built a lab-scale representation of an atmosphere using a meter-scale rotating annular tank. The outer bottom edge of the tank gets heated&#8211;representing the sun&#8217;s warming at the equator&#8211;while a pipe in the center of the tank gets cooled near the tank surface, which mimics the chilling effect of the poles. Researchers filled the tank with a water-glycerol mixture and recorded how their artificial atmosphere responded at different rotation rates.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-full"><img fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" width="720" height="360" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/geo_model_ani.gif" alt="Two different rotating atmospheres, colored by vorticity (red clockwise, blue counterclockwise). The left version has a slower rate of rotation, and thus larger length scales." class="wp-image-29754"/><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Two different rotating atmospheres, colored by vorticity (red clockwise, blue counterclockwise). The left version has a slower rate of rotation, and thus larger length scales.</figcaption></figure>



<p>The results show an energy spectrum that&#8217;s consistent with atmospheric observations&#8211;with a steep drop at large length scales and a flatter one at smaller scales. But interestingly, they also found that the cascade was temperature-dependent in ways that current models don&#8217;t predict. Untangling that effect could help us understand not only our atmosphere but those of other planets. (Image credit: tank &#8211; H. Scolan, animation &#8211; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/n2nj-dg5r">S. Ding et al.</a>; research credit: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/n2nj-dg5r">S. Ding et al.</a>; via <a href="https://physics.aps.org/articles/v19/40?__readwiseLocation=">APS</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>Bouncing on a Wave</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/bouncing-on-a-wave/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/bouncing-on-a-wave/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 29 Apr 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Phenomena]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[2025gofm]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[bouncing droplets]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[coalescence]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[droplets]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[hydrodynamic quantum analogs]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[quantum mechanics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>

		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=29790</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[On a vibrating fluid, droplets can bounce and interact in complex ways. Here, researchers demonstrate some of the peculiar dynamics of these wave-guided droplets, showing how they can do things like pair up in waltzes. To keep the droplets from coalescing with one another, they perform their experiments in a pressurized chamber; the higher air [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/wave_waltz1-1024x576.png" title="Droplets bouncing on a vibrating fluid surface. Text reads, &quot;This is a collection of walking droplets bouncing on the surface of a vertically vibrated fluid interface...&quot;" alt="Droplets bouncing on a vibrating fluid surface. Text reads, &quot;This is a collection of walking droplets bouncing on the surface of a vertically vibrated fluid interface...&quot;" /></div></div>



<p> On a <a href="/tagged/vibration">vibrating</a> fluid, <a href="/tagged/bouncing-droplets/">droplets can bounce</a> and interact in complex ways. Here, researchers demonstrate some of the peculiar dynamics of these wave-guided droplets, showing how they can do things like pair up in waltzes. To keep the droplets from <a href="/tagged/coalescence/">coalescing</a> with one another, they perform their experiments in a pressurized chamber; the higher air pressure makes it harder for the air film between droplets to drain during a collision, making the droplets unable to coalesce. Under these conditions, the authors show that the droplet-wave system has <a href="/tagged/hydrodynamic-quantum-analogs/">quantum-like statistics</a>. (Video and image credit: J. Clampett et al.)</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>&#8220;Sidewall Symphony&#8221;</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/sidewall-symphony/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/sidewall-symphony/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 28 Apr 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[2025gofm]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[flow visualization]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluids as art]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[turbulence]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=28631</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Flow visualization is both an art and science in fluid dynamics. Here, researchers were interested in studying the separation bubble that forms over a backward-facing ramp&#8211;a shape that shows up, for example, on an aircraft. In these areas, the flow over the surface separates, leaving an unsteady, recirculating bubble. That&#8217;s the flow that researchers are [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p><a href="/tagged/flow-visualization/">Flow visualization</a> is both an art and science in fluid dynamics. Here, researchers were interested in studying the <a href="/tagged/flow-separation/">separation bubble</a> that forms over a backward-facing ramp&#8211;a shape that shows up, for example, on an aircraft. In these areas, the flow over the surface separates, leaving an unsteady, recirculating bubble. </p>



<p>That&#8217;s the flow that researchers are visualizing here. They&#8217;ve done so by adding tiny helium-filled soap bubbles to the flow. With bright lights illuminating the bubbles, each one leaves a streak in a photograph, showing where the bubble moved during the time the camera&#8217;s shutter was open. Although images like these are beautiful, they can also be analyzed by computers to extract  the underlying flow that created the image. (Image and research credit: <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-fluid-mechanics/article/threedimensional-lowfrequency-dynamics-of-a-turbulent-separation-bubble/4ABB5AA0338669640C5374D52E0BA58E#article">B. Steinfurth et al.</a>; see also <a href="https://gfm.aps.org/meetings/dfd-2025/692e39e3a7f805227b16fe68">here</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-large"><img decoding="async" width="1024" height="723" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/sidewall_symphony_main-1024x723.png" alt="A research poster showing streaks left by hydrogen bubbles in the flow over a backward-facing ramp." class="wp-image-28633" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/sidewall_symphony_main-1024x723.png 1024w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/sidewall_symphony_main-300x212.png 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/sidewall_symphony_main-768x542.png 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/sidewall_symphony_main-1536x1085.png 1536w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/sidewall_symphony_main.png 1600w" sizes="(max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px" /></figure>
]]></content:encoded>

The tiny organisms may be visible only under a microscope, but gatherings like these stretch hundreds of kilometers and are visible from space. Like tracer particles in a flow, the phytoplankton outline the swirls [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p>Peeking between the clouds, satellites caught a glimpse of a massive <a href="/tagged/phytoplankton/">phytoplankton</a> bloom off the coast of Greenland in May 2024. The tiny organisms may be visible only under a microscope, but gatherings like these stretch hundreds of kilometers and are visible from space. Like <a href="/tagged/flow-visualization/">tracer particles in a flow</a>, the phytoplankton outline the swirls and eddies of the underlying ocean. (Image credit: L. Dauphin; via <a href="https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/152953/peek-a-bloom-in-the-north-atlantic">NASA Earth Observatory</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img decoding="async" width="1024" height="682" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main-1024x682.png" alt="A satellite image reveals the blue and green swirls of a phytoplankton bloom." class="wp-image-21903" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main-1024x682.png 1024w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main-300x200.png 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main-768x512.png 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main-1536x1024.png 1536w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main-270x180.png 270w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main-710x473.png 710w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/greenlandbloom_amo_20240616_lrg_main.png 2000w" sizes="(max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">A satellite image reveals the blue and green swirls of a phytoplankton bloom.</figcaption></figure>

		<item>
		<title>Viscoelastic Vortex Street</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/viscoelastic-vortex-street/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/viscoelastic-vortex-street/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 23 Apr 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[flow visualization]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluids as art]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[viscoelasticity]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[von Karman vortex street]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[vortex shedding]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=28357</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[When flow moves past a cylinder, vortices get shed in its wake. Known as a von Karman vortex street, this distinctive pattern is seen behind flags, islands, and even behind starships. Here, researchers are simulating flow of a viscoelastic fluid, where&#8211;unlike water or other Newtonian fluids&#8211;elastic stresses can build up. As the flow hits the [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p>When flow moves past a cylinder, vortices get shed in its wake. Known as a <a href="/tagged/von-Karman-vortex-street/">von Karman vortex street</a>, this distinctive pattern is seen behind <a href="/2012/08/the-flapping-of-flexible-objects-like-flags-have/">flags</a>, <a href="/2022/01/swirls-in-the-wake/">islands</a>, and even <a href="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2016/09/fuckyeahfluiddynamics-todays-post-is-largely/">behind starships</a>. Here, researchers are simulating flow of a <a href="/tagged/viscoelasticity/">viscoelastic fluid</a>, where&#8211;unlike water or other Newtonian fluids&#8211;elastic stresses can build up. </p>



<p>As the flow hits the leading edge of the cylinder, the polymers in the fluid compress and then get stretched as the flow moves around the cylinder. The left image shows vorticity in the flow; the right shows elastic stresses. The large swirls are primary vortices&#8211;those shed off the cylinder. But look closely and you&#8217;ll see smaller secondary vortices curled up beside the primaries. These form when the elastic stresses in the fluid pull some of the shear layer into the wake. (Image and research credit: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/dsx8-n7mr">U. Patel et al.</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-full"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1000" height="919" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/viscoelastic_VIV_main.png" alt="Simulation of a flow around a cylinder in a viscoelastic flow. Left, vorticity; right, elastic stresses." class="wp-image-28359" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/viscoelastic_VIV_main.png 1000w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/viscoelastic_VIV_main-300x276.png 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/viscoelastic_VIV_main-768x706.png 768w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></figure>
]]></content:encoded>

		<post-id xmlns="com-wordpress:feed-additions:1">28357</post-id>	</item>
		<item>
		<title>Understanding Fish and Turbines</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/understanding-fish-and-turbines/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/understanding-fish-and-turbines/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 22 Apr 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Phenomena]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[2025gofm]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[biology]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[computational fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fish]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[flow visualization]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[large eddy simulation]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[turbulence]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=28569</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Fish detect turbulence in the water around them; among other things, this helps them avoid colliding with objects. Here, researchers are looking to understand how fish interact with underwater turbines. Experiments give them a set of trajectories that actual fish follow when dealing with the experimental turbine. But to understand what the fish is detecting, [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/fish_turb1-1024x576.png" title="Illustration of a fish encountering an underwater turbine. Text reads, &quot;Fish detect turbulence signals using the lateral line system. Turbulence as viscous hydrodynamic disturbances.&quot;" alt="Illustration of a fish encountering an underwater turbine. Text reads, &quot;Fish detect turbulence signals using the lateral line system. Turbulence as viscous hydrodynamic disturbances.&quot;" /></div></div>



<p><a href="/tagged/fish/">Fish</a> detect <a href="/tagged/turbulence/">turbulence</a> in the water around them; among other things, this helps them avoid colliding with objects. Here, researchers are looking to understand how fish interact with underwater turbines. Experiments give them a set of trajectories that actual fish follow when dealing with the experimental turbine. But to understand what the fish is detecting, the researchers build a digital facsimile of the turbine and use <a href="/tagged/large-eddy-simulation/">Large Eddy Simulation</a> (LES) to calculate the turbine&#8217;s wake. </p>



<p>By overlaying the fish trajectories onto the simulated flow structures, they can better understand what flows the fish is and is not comfortable with. That knowledge helps engineers design turbines with smaller ecological impact. (Video and image credit: <a href="https://gfm.aps.org/meetings/dfd-2025/692e39eba7f805227b16ff4c">H. Seyedzadeh et al.</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>A Fungus That Freezes Water</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/a-fungus-that-freezes-water/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/a-fungus-that-freezes-water/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 21 Apr 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[biology]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[freezing]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[supercooling]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=29746</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Although water can freeze below 0 degrees Celsius, it requires a little help&#8211;in the form of a nucleation site&#8211;to do so. Often temperatures must dip well below 0 degrees Celsius for droplets to become ice. But a new study shows that at least one fungus forms proteins that help the process along. The proteins come [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p>Although water can freeze below 0 degrees Celsius, it requires a little help&#8211;in the form of a nucleation site&#8211;to do so. Often temperatures must dip well below 0 degrees Celsius for droplets to become ice. But a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aed9652">new study shows</a> that at least one fungus forms proteins that help the process along.</p>



<p>The proteins come from the <em>Mortierellaceae</em>  fungal family, by way of a bacterial species some hundreds of thousands of years ago or more. In experiments, adding the fungal protein helped water freeze 10 or more degrees Celsius sooner than it otherwise would. </p>



<p>The authors note that there are many possible applications for this freezing additive; it could help preserve food or cells without requiring lower freezing temperatures that could damage delicate tissues. It could also serve as a cloud seeding chemical in place of toxic silver iodide particles. (Image and research credit: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aed9652">R. Eufemio et al.</a>; via <a href="https://gizmodo.com/this-fungus-can-make-water-freeze-2000733992?__readwiseLocation=">Gizmodo</a>; see also <a href="https://news.vt.edu/articles/2026/03/ice-nucleation-fungi-boris-vinatzer-xiaofeng-wang.html">V. Tech</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>Shocking Fizzy Jets</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/shocking-fizzy-jets/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/04/shocking-fizzy-jets/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 20 Apr 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Phenomena]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[Many industrial processes break a fluid jet into droplets, like spray painting and ink-jet printing. Here, researchers examine an effervescent fluid jet made up of both liquid and gas. Like a fluid-only jet, this fizzy jet forms sheets, bags, ligaments, and droplets. As it breaks down, it creates a range of droplet sizes&#8211;both large and [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/fizzy_jet1-1024x576.png" title="An effervescent jet made up of many droplets and ligaments of fluid." alt="An effervescent jet made up of many droplets and ligaments of fluid." /></div></div>



<p>Many industrial processes break a fluid jet into droplets, like spray painting and ink-jet printing. Here, researchers examine an effervescent fluid jet made up of both liquid and gas. Like a fluid-only jet, this fizzy jet forms sheets, bags, ligaments, and droplets. As it breaks down, it creates a range of droplet sizes&#8211;both large and small. But when a <a href="/tagged/shockwave">shock wave</a> passes, the jet and its droplets get atomized into even tinier droplets. (Video and image credit: <a href="https://gfm.aps.org/meetings/dfd-2025/692e39eba7f805227b16ff3d">S. Rao et al.</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>
